title: How Acceptance and Commitment Therapy Helps You Find Your Own Compass of Values
excerpt: We often decide out of fear of disappointing others. The ideas behind ACT offer another route: name your values, make room for what gets in the way, and act from what matters.

value.text: Many of our decisions are shaped less by what we want than by what we are trying to avoid. We take on the project because saying no would look ungrateful. We stay because leaving would disappoint someone. Then we wonder why a life full of good things can feel so strangely airless. From the outside everything is in order. From the inside, it is somebody else's order.

Acceptance and Commitment Therapy, usually shortened to ACT, starts somewhere else. ACT is a model that grew out of research in clinical psychology; I draw on its ideas in counselling rather than offering it as a finished programme. Instead of asking you to feel differently before you are allowed to act, it asks a simpler question: given that doubt and old habits will come along for the ride anyway, which direction do you actually want to travel in? That direction is what ACT calls values, and finding yours is much of what inner clarity turns out to mean.

A goal is something you complete and tick off: the promotion, the half marathon, the move abroad. A value is a quality of action you can keep choosing for the rest of your life — honesty, curiosity, courage, being a steady presence for the people closest to you. Goals are places on a map. Values are the bearing you travel by.

This is quietly liberating. Goals can fail; a value can only be neglected, never taken from you. If you value connection and a friendship ends, connection is still available to you tomorrow. Build your sense of self entirely on goals and every setback becomes an identity crisis. Let it rest on values and setbacks still hurt, but they no longer leave you without a direction.
Finding your values is less about inventing them than noticing what is already there:

items: The moments you feel most like yourself — what quality were you bringing to them?
What you quietly envy in others, which often points at something you have shelved.
What reliably makes you angry; anger frequently stands guard over a value that was stepped on.
The small choices you are proud of even though nobody noticed them.
How you would want to be remembered for the way you were with people, not for what you achieved.

value.text: Unhooking from the thoughts that run the show

ACT uses the term cognitive defusion. It sounds technical and means something quite ordinary: learning to hold your own thoughts more loosely. Thoughts arrive all day long in the voice of fact. "I am not the kind of person who does that." "If I disappoint them, it will be unforgivable." We rarely examine these sentences. We simply obey them.

Defusion is the shift from being inside a thought to noticing that you are having one. In practice it can be as small as four extra words: not "I am going to make a fool of myself" but "I am having the thought that I am going to make a fool of myself." The content is unchanged. What changes is the room around it — and room is precisely what you need in order to choose. The aim is never to argue with the thought or swap it for a nicer one, only to stop letting it drive.
Making room for what you cannot argue away

The other half of the model is willingness, sometimes called acceptance, and it is the part people most often misread. It does not mean approving of difficult feelings, or resigning yourself to a situation that needs to change. It means dropping the second, exhausting struggle: the fight against the fact that you feel what you feel.

Most of us pour enormous energy into that second struggle — bracing, distracting, over-preparing, rehearsing conversations at three in the morning. The paradox ACT points at is that the effort not to feel something usually keeps it in the room for longer. Making room is not passive; it is a deliberate loosening of the grip, and it frees up energy that was going nowhere. For the physiological side of this, my [plain-English guide to the nervous system](/blog/nervous-system-plain-english-guide) pairs well with it.
Small steps, and decisions that finally feel clear

Values without action stay decorative. Committed action means translating a direction into steps small enough that you will genuinely take them this week: one sentence said plainly in a meeting, the laptop left in another room for a single evening, the message you have been drafting in your head for a month. Ten small value-aligned steps do more for a sense of integrity than one heroic gesture followed by three months of nothing. This is often where the gap between [functioning well and feeling well](/blog/functioning-well-vs-feeling-well) begins to close.

People rarely arrive with an impossible decision because the options are genuinely equal. It is that every option has quietly been rewritten as a question about who will be upset. When the question changes — from which choice keeps everyone comfortable to which choice moves me toward what matters — decision-making seldom becomes easy, but it usually becomes clear. Clarity and ease are not the same thing, and clarity is the one that lasts.
You do not have to feel ready in order to move in the direction you have chosen. Readiness usually arrives afterwards, if at all.

Much of our work together in [psychological counselling](/work-with-me/psychological-counselling) is exactly this: separating your own values from the expectations you have absorbed, then working out what a life organised around the former would ask of you. It is often most useful in the middle of a transition, which is why I wrote about [why big life changes feel harder than they should](/blog/why-big-life-changes-feel-harder). If any of it sounds familiar, you can read about [how I work](/about) or simply [get in touch](/contact) — you do not need to arrive with your values already sorted.
